tldr: This paper proposes a two-wheeled quadrotor that can drive along walls and floors while keeping a completely level attitude without extra actuators, achieved by fixing all four rotors at a tilted angle and spinning them in the same clockwise direction.
hero_caption: Overall coordinate frames and configuration of the proposed two-wheeled quadrotor. Equipped with passive wheels on both sides, it achieves stable locomotion in contact with surfaces as well as aerial flight.
overview:
Drones (quadrotors) are widely used for infrastructure inspection and disaster response, but generating horizontal force fundamentally requires them to tilt their bodies. However, when inspecting walls or floors using wheels, having the vehicle tilt while driving can lead to blurred camera views or physical interference. On the other hand, adding dedicated servo motors (tilt mechanisms) to tilt the rotors increases weight and mechanical complexity.

To address this, the authors proposed an unconventional approach: fixing the rotors at a preset tilt and leveraging the contact constraints of the wheels. Surprisingly, instead of alternating clockwise and counterclockwise rotations as conventional drones do (the PNPN configuration), they adopted a unique configuration where all four rotors spin clockwise (the 4P configuration). Using control theory, they revealed that under surface contact constraints, this 4P configuration prevents cancelations and generates greater propulsion along the floor.

In simulation, the proposed vehicle hovered in free space just like a conventional drone. Furthermore, during horizontal floor locomotion where a standard wheeled drone tilted its pitch angle by more than 18 degrees, the proposed design smoothly traversed the floor while maintaining an almost perfectly level attitude with a pitch deviation of under 0.75 degrees.
contributions: Formulated and analyzed the controllability and feasible thrust of a two-wheeled quadrotor under contact constraints with general surfaces (such as floors and walls) using control theory.

Optimized a vehicle design combining an all-identical spin direction (4P configuration) with half-turn symmetric fixed tilt angles to directly generate tangential propulsion while maintaining a level attitude.
Mathematically proved that the 4P configuration secures larger maximum propulsion and a larger hovering margin during contact locomotion than the conventional alternating (PNPN) configuration.
Demonstrated in MuJoCo simulations that the vehicle achieves both aerial hovering and horizontal floor locomotion while maintaining a level attitude without adding any extra actuators.

sections.heading: How wheels and tilted rotors shape the vehicle's dynamics
sections.summary: This section models the kinematics of the two-wheeled quadrotor, the thrust-to-wrench mapping matrix from the fixed-tilted rotors, and the contact constraint dynamics when the wheels touch down. The wheels are passive with no drive motors, so all locomotive thrust is generated directly by the rotors.
sections.details:
This section establishes the equations of motion underlying the proposed two-wheeled drone.

### II-A Coordinates and Kinematics
A body-fixed frame $\Sigma_b$ is placed at the vehicle's center and the wheel axle midpoint, while an inertial frame $\Sigma_w$ is defined in space. The vehicle mass is $m$, the inertia tensor is $\bm{J}$, the wheel radius is $r_w$, and the distance from the axle center to each wheel is $\ell_w$.

### II-B Rotor Wrench Map
A mapping matrix $\bm{M}$ transforms the thrust $f_i$ and reaction torque (with spin-direction coefficient $\kappa_i$) of each rotor into a 6-DOF wrench acting on the vehicle. Here, clockwise is denoted as P (Positive) and counterclockwise as N (Negative). In this vehicle, each rotor is fixed with a tilt angle $\beta_i$ around axes parallel to the wheel axle ($y$-axis), allowing direct force generation along the forward heading ($x$-axis). The lateral thrust component is zero ($\bm{M}_{f,y}=\bm{0}$).

### II-C Constraint Dynamics
Three geometric and nonholonomic constraints are applied to model contact with a surface (normal vector $\bm{n}$): maintaining contact height, zero lateral wheel slip, and keeping the wheel axle parallel to the surface. These reduce the permissible velocity space to three dimensions: forward translation, pitch rotation, and yaw rotation around the surface normal. The constraint forces enter the dynamics via Lagrange multipliers $\lambda_1$ (normal force), $\lambda_2$ (lateral friction), and $\lambda_3$ (torque from load differences between the two wheels).

captions.F2: Geometric arrangement of the fixed-tilted rotors. Each rotor is tilted by an angle $\beta_i$ around an axis parallel to the wheel axle, generating propulsion along the heading ($b_x$-axis) without tilting the vehicle body.

sections.heading: Can it move freely while staying grounded? Contact-mode controllability
sections.summary: The authors analyze whether the constrained vehicle can be steered as intended. They derive the rank condition required to directly drive the three reduced degrees of freedom using rotor thrusts alone without tilting the body, and establish contact margin conditions to keep the wheels grounded.
sections.details:
When its wheels are on the ground, a drone behaves very differently from when it is airborne. This section explores whether the vehicle remains stable and controllable in this "contact mode."

### III-A Controllability of Unconstrained Subspace
By projecting onto the constraints to eliminate the multipliers, the permissible 3D reduced dynamics are derived. In the state equation linearized around a nominal attitude $\bm{R}_\ast$, the authors prove that if the reduced wrench map $\tilde{\bm{M}}(\bm{R}_\ast)$ has rank 3, arbitrary reduced accelerations can be achieved directly through thrust inputs alone without relying on pitch gravity coupling (controllability).

### III-B Contact Maintenance in Constrained Subspace
A quasi-static contact margin $m_c^{\rm qs}(\bm{u})$ is defined to ensure the wheels neither lose ground contact nor slip laterally. In addition to positive normal forces and friction limits, both wheels must stay grounded (the roll torque must remain within the limits supported by the wheel baseline and normal load).

### III-C Contact-Mode Hoverability
A vehicle is defined as "contact-mode hoverable" if an equilibrium state exists where thrust inputs do not saturate, the contact margin stays positive, and controllability holds. A hovering margin $\gamma^\star$ is introduced to quantify this balance as the optimal value of a linear program (LP).

sections.heading: Why spinning all rotors in the same direction (4P) wins: Structure and tilt optimization
sections.summary: Focusing on horizontal floor locomotion, the tilt angles and rotor spin directions were optimized. The results show that the 4P configuration, where all four rotors rotate clockwise, achieves greater propulsion (about 1.6 times higher) and a larger hovering margin than the conventional alternating PNPN configuration.
sections.details:
### IV-A Symmetric Tilt Design and Rank Condition
When designing tilt angles, tilting symmetrically across the $y$-$z$ plane causes a rank deficiency that prevents direct horizontal thrust. In contrast, adopting a half-turn (180-degree rotational) symmetry around the vehicle center achieves full rank (rank 3). Under this symmetry, the spin directions narrow down to either all-identical (4P) or alternating (PNPN).

### IV-B Feasible Wrench Set
The maximum tangential force (propulsion) $\bar{f}_t$ achievable without disrupting attitude equilibrium or lifting wheels is formulated as an optimization problem over a convex polytope.

### IV-C Structure and Tilt Optimization
A multi-objective optimization problem was solved considering the maximization of $\bar{f}_t$, the hovering margin, small tilt angles (to retain aerial flight efficiency), and the condition number of the control allocation matrix. Comparing parameters for a 1.10 kg vehicle with 4.78 N maximum rotor thrust yielded:
- Optimal tilt angles: $[-9.74^\circ, 28.28^\circ]$ for 4P, and $[-21.16^\circ, 5.29^\circ]$ for PNPN.
- Maximum traction $\bar{f}_t$: $1.205\,\mathrm{N}$ for 4P versus $0.751\,\mathrm{N}$ for PNPN, showing a significant advantage for 4P.
- Hovering margin $\gamma^\star$: 2.210 for 4P compared to 1.539 for PNPN.

The 4P configuration wins because of how reaction torques and tilt-induced yaw moments interact. By leveraging the wheel contact forces (roll resistance), the 4P setup maintains a large propulsion envelope across a wide range of small tilt angles.

captions.F4: Comparison of maximum traction force $\bar{f}_t$ distributions across the tilt-angle plane. (a)-(b) show the conventional PNPN configuration, while (c)-(d) show the proposed 4P configuration. Red points mark optimal solutions. The 4P setup achieves both a higher peak value and a broader region of high propulsion at relatively small tilt angles.

sections.heading: Switching between aerial flight and level ground-locomotion control
sections.summary: Controllers were developed for aerial hovering and ground locomotion. Because the proposed 4P vehicle does not need to pitch to move forward on the ground, thrust and yaw moments are allocated independently while maintaining a completely level target attitude (roll = 0, pitch = 0).
sections.details:
### V-A Hovering Controller
During free flight, a geometric PD controller on $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ computes the required forces and moments, which are mapped to rotor thrusts via matrix inversion. Both configurations share this controller structure to ensure a fair comparison.

### V-B Ground Locomotion Controller
During surface locomotion, wheels provide gravity compensation, so vertical flight thrust is not needed for lift. Vertical thrust is set to a constant $\bar{f}_z$ to optimize traction.
- **Standard type (non-tilted, PNPN):** Unable to generate lateral force directly, it must pitch forward just as in aerial flight to propel itself.
- **Proposed type (4P, tilted):** Capable of driving while keeping a level attitude (roll = 0, pitch = 0). The thrust allocation is solved algebraically using an invertible $4\times 4$ matrix. If actuator limits or wheel-lift constraints are reached, it transitions to a constrained least-squares allocation via a small quadratic program (QP) to guarantee a safety margin $\underline{m}>0$.

sections.heading: Simulation validation: Proving aerial hovering and level-attitude driving
sections.summary: Using the MuJoCo physics simulator, the proposed design was compared with a standard vehicle in both free flight and floor locomotion scenarios. The proposed vehicle maintained stable aerial hovering performance while limiting pitch angle variation to less than 0.75 degrees during ground locomotion, demonstrating virtually level-attitude driving.
sections.details:
The proposed 4P tilted drone was evaluated against a standard non-tilted wheeled drone using the MuJoCo physics engine.

### Aerial Hovering Performance
When commanded to ascend to 1.2 m and translate horizontally to $x=0.6\,\mathrm{m}$, the proposed vehicle exhibited trajectory tracking and attitude stability nearly identical to the standard vehicle. This confirmed that tilting the rotors does not impair flight performance.

### Ground Locomotion Performance
A point-to-point test was conducted to drive 1.2 m in the $x$ direction from a standstill. Both vehicles converged to the goal position, but the proposed vehicle demonstrated better response with an overshoot of 9.9% (peak at 1.318 m) compared to 17.2% for the standard vehicle (peak at 1.406 m).

The difference in attitude response was striking. The standard drone had to tilt sharply to accelerate and decelerate, with pitch angles varying between $-8.96^\circ$ and $18.20^\circ$. In contrast, the proposed drone stayed level, keeping roll angles within $0.005^\circ$ and pitch variations under $0.75^\circ$. Despite a minor yaw deviation of around $2^\circ$, it numerically validated high-speed locomotion while maintaining a nearly level posture.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what comes next
sections.summary: Combining an all-clockwise rotor spin (4P configuration) with fixed-tilt angles creates a new two-wheeled quadrotor that drives along surfaces without body tilt. Its advantages were verified through both theoretical analysis and simulation.
sections.details: This paper introduced a novel two-wheeled UAV that uses surface contact constraints to generate propulsion without tilting its body. Through reduced-wrench analysis, the authors revealed that a 4P rotor configuration produces greater tangential force than the conventional PNPN setup. MuJoCo simulations validated that the vehicle retains hovering capability while driving across surfaces with minimal attitude changes. Free of extra servo mechanisms, this lightweight and mechanically simple approach offers a practical design for contact-based inspection in tight infrastructure spaces.

takeaways: Under contact constraints (wheels on the ground), the conventional wisdom of flight (that alternating PNPN is best) does not always hold; an all-identical rotation (4P) can yield larger propulsion and wider margins.
Adopting a half-turn (180-degree) symmetric fixed-tilt configuration allows direct translational force generation while keeping the vehicle level, without needing extra servos or mechanisms.
Modeling contact margins (preventing wheel lift and lateral slip) as a convex polytope wrench set enables control allocation to be cast as an efficient quadratic program (QP).
limitations: The approach has only been validated in physics simulations (MuJoCo); real-world hardware experiments and robustness against environmental disturbances remain untested.
A yaw deviation of around 2 degrees occurred during driving, indicating that further compensation or controller tuning is required for strictly straight tracking.
Because the rotors have fixed tilt angles, energy efficiency during purely vertical hovering is slightly reduced compared to conventional drones with vertical rotors.
